title: The Muddy Mystery on the Lily Pad
markdown:
In a pond so sparkly it looked like a giant glitter bomb had gone off lived two best friends. Cattails that sang happy tunes. Dragonflies that zipped like tiny shimmery helicopters. Puddle, a duck with feet the colour of sunshine, loved to flap and quack and waddle with all his might. Fern, a frog with eyes like shiny green jewels, could leap farther than Puddle could flap.

Every year the pond friends had a big splashy concert. Not just any concert — the biggest, most musical, most wobbly-kneed event of the whole summer. Fish blew bubbles in time. The crickets chirped a special song. Even the water lilies seemed to sway like dancers in long green dresses. And the stage? The biggest lily pad of all, a giant round green stage right in the middle of the pond. Everyone practiced their songs and dances for weeks, making sure notes were perfect and steps were super-duper. Puddle was practicing his wiggliest, giggliest Quacky-Doo dance. Fern was practicing his deep rumbling croak-solo, which sounded like happy thunder mixed with a cozy sigh.

But one sunny morning, as they waddled and hopped onto the stage for a quick practice, they stopped. Tiny muddy footprints. All over. Small smudgy marks, as if someone had walked through a puddle and then done a little happy dance.

“Quack-tastrophe,” squawked Puddle, yellow feet doing a confused dance all by themselves. “The concert is tonight. The stage is supposed to be shiny clean, not muddy-muddles.”

Fern hopped closer, big green eyes blinking slowly. “These are very small. Too small for a big bear or even a wobbly badger. Light and fast.” He scanned the edges, then the sparkly water. “Someone is making a mess before our big show.”

Therefore they opened the Puddle and Fern Detective Agency. Motto, which Puddle sometimes forgot and Fern always remembered: We’ll find you, even if we have to paddle all day and night.

Their first stop was Mrs. Dragonfly, busy making her see-through wings extra sparkly. She always knew everything. “Excuse us, Mrs. Dragonfly, queen of the sky,” chirped Puddle, trying to sound important. “Did you see anyone leaving muddy footprints on the lily-pad stage this morning?”

Mrs. Dragonfly zoomed around their heads in a dazzling blur. “Muddy footprints? Goodness gracious, no. I was too busy looking at my own beautiful reflection. I only see teeny-tiny specks of dust on my own wings, and I keep them perfectly clean, thank you very much. Way too clean for mud.” A proud flutter.

Therefore they waddled and hopped to Llinos the Beaver, chomping a very big log. Llinos was always busy. “Llinos,” called Fern, a clear deep croak. “Have you seen any muddy visitors near the concert stage?”

Llinos paused, a piece of wood hanging from his mouth. Whiskery nose twitching. “Mmmph. Nope. The only mud I see is the kind I’m using for my dam. And that’s staying right here, holding my home together. Can’t have my dam washing away.” A determined nod, back to chomping.

Puddle and Fern felt a little sad, noses drooped. The trail of muddy prints got fainter, leading away from the stage toward the tall swishy reeds at the pond’s edge. They pushed through the green stalks, water tickling their legs. Fern stopped, webbed hand up. “Look.”

Hiding behind a patch of soft damp moss, sunshine peeking through the reeds, was a tiny trembling creature. A mouse, no bigger than Puddle’s biggest webbed foot. Fur the colour of warm dirt. Whiskers twitched. Nose wiggled nervously. So shy, and a little sad.

Puddle, forgetting the footprints for a moment, waddled closer, yellow feet hardly marking the soft ground. “Hello, little one.” Soft quack. “Are you okay? You look a little worried.”

The mouse let out a tiny startled squeak and tried to curl even smaller.

“We’re not grumpy,” croaked Fern, voice like a warm hug. “We’re just trying to find who made those muddy footprints. Not mad. Curious.”

The little mouse peeked from behind its paws. Eyes like two shiny black buttons. It looked from Puddle’s friendly beak to Fern’s gentle smile. Then it did something amazing. A tiny musical squeak. And then it started to dance.

It twirled and leaped, little paws tapping a super-fast rhythm on the damp ground, leaving more muddy footprints. It spun, jumped, even did a wiggle-step that made Puddle and Fern giggle.

They stared, mouths hanging open. The little mouse was not trying to be naughty. It was practicing. So full of happy wiggles it could not help dancing wherever it went, even if it made a little mess.

“You love to dance, don’t you?” Puddle quacked softly. Confusion melted into understanding. He had never seen such happy dancing.

The mouse nodded super-fast, whiskers a blur, and managed a tiny shy bow.

“That was absolutely wonderful,” said Fern, eyes twinkling. “You move like a leaf on the wind. What’s your name?”

“Squeaky,” the mouse whispered, barely a puff of air.

“Well, Squeaky,” said Puddle, a happy flap that sent tiny droplets up. “You’ve been practicing so hard. And we have our big concert tonight.”

Fern’s wide froggy grin. “Would you like to dance on the big lily-pad stage? Show everyone your moves?”

Squeaky’s eyes widened. “Me? Dance? In front of everyone?”

“Of course,” quacked Puddle, a little nudge with his beak. “You’re the best dancer we’ve seen. And don’t worry about the mud. We can all help clean it up.”

Therefore they worked together. A funny sight. Puddle scooped wet leaves with his beak. Fern splashed with webbed feet, washing the last muddy trails. Squeaky scurried, wiping leftover smudges with a soft bit of fluff. They giggled as they worked.

When the sun began to set, orange, pink, and purple, a golden glow across the pond, the Lily-Pad Concert began. Mrs. Dragonfly sparkled in the twilight. Llinos tapped his tail to the beat. Fish blew little bubbles of applause.

Then it was Squeaky’s turn. He hopped onto the stage, his heart thumping like a tiny drum. He took a deep breath, looked at his new friends Puddle and Fern, and danced. He twirled and leaped and tap-danced with such pure joy and energy that everyone gasped. He did flips and spins, he shuffled and hopped, and he looked happier than anyone had ever seen him. The most wonderful joyful dancing the pond had watched in years.

Puddle quacked with delight. Fern gave a loud rumbling croak of joy. Squeaky was not shy anymore. Those muddy footprints had led to the concert’s best surprise.

Afterward they sat on the clean pad, feet still a little damp, and Squeaky practiced one more tiny bow for tomorrow, in case the pond asked him back.
